segments.text: Hi, I'm Lan. Are you new here?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, I am. My name is Tom.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Nice to meet you, Tom. Where are you from?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I'm from Canada. I live near the school now.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Oh, I live near the school too.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Great! We can walk to class together.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Good morning. What would you like?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Can I have a tea, please?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Hot or iced?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Hot, please. And a small cake.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That's four dollars.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Here you are. Thank you.
Hello, my name is Mai.
There are four people in my family.
My father is a teacher and my mother is a nurse.
I have one brother. His name is Nam.
He is ten years old and he likes football.
On Sundays, we have dinner at my grandmother's house.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Hello. Do you have apples today?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yes, we have red apples and green apples.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: How much are the red apples?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: They are two dollars a kilo.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: OK, one kilo of red apples, please. And three bananas.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Sure. That's three dollars and fifty cents.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Excuse me. Where is the post office?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: It's on Green Street, next to the bank.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Is it far from here?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: No, it's about five minutes on foot.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Do I turn left or right at the corner?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Turn right, then go straight.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Thank you very much.

a1-test2.title: A1 · A message from a friend

segments.text: Hi Anna, it's Ben.
I'm at the cinema, but the film starts at seven, not six.
Can you come at a quarter to seven?
I have the tickets.
After the film, let's eat pizza.
Call me back, OK? Bye!

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Good afternoon, Rosa's Restaurant.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Hi, I'd like to book a table for Saturday evening.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Of course. For how many people?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: For six, please. It's my mother's birthday.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: We have a table at eight o'clock. Is that OK?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Perfect. Could we sit near the window?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Sure. Can I have your name, please?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: It's David Clark.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Are you doing anything this weekend, Sara?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I'm going to visit my aunt in the countryside on Saturday.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That sounds nice. How are you getting there?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: By train. It takes about two hours.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Will you be back on Sunday?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yes, in the afternoon. Why?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: There's a concert in the park on Sunday evening. Do you want to come?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I'd love to!
Welcome aboard the City Explorer bus tour.
The tour takes ninety minutes and makes six stops.
Our first stop is the old market, where you can try local food.
You can get off at any stop and catch the next bus thirty minutes later.
Please keep your ticket with you, because the driver will check it.
Free water is available at the front of the bus.
Enjoy the tour!

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Excuse me, when is the next train to Brighton?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: The next one leaves at ten fifteen from platform four.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Oh, I have to wait forty minutes. Is there an earlier bus?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, there's a bus at nine fifty, but it takes longer.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: How much longer?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: About half an hour more than the train.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Then I'll take the train. One single ticket, please.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That's twelve pounds.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Good morning. What seems to be the problem?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I've had a bad headache for three days, and I feel tired all the time.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Are you sleeping well?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Not really. I've been working late every night this week.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I think you need more rest. Try to go to bed before eleven.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Should I take any medicine?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: You can take this for the headache, twice a day after meals.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Thank you, doctor.
Here is the weather for the weekend.
On Saturday morning it will be cloudy, with some rain in the afternoon.
Temperatures will reach about fifteen degrees.
Sunday will be much better, with sunshine all day.
It will also be warmer, around twenty degrees.
So if you are planning a picnic, Sunday is the day to do it.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Thanks for coming in, James. Can you tell me why you applied for this job?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Sure. I've worked in a shop for two years, and I want to move into marketing.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: What do you think you are good at?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I'm good at talking to customers, and I enjoy working in a team.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: This job sometimes means working at weekends. Would that be a problem?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Not at all. My weekends are usually free.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Great. We'll let you know our decision by Friday.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Hi, I bought these headphones here last week, but the left side has stopped working.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Do you have the receipt?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, here it is.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Thank you. Would you like a replacement or your money back?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I'd prefer a replacement, if you have the same model.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Let me check. Yes, we have one in black, but not in white.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Black is fine.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Here you are. If there's another problem, you can bring them back within a year.
Many students study for hours but still forget what they learned.
Here are three simple tips that can help.
First, study in short sessions of about thirty minutes, then take a five-minute break.
Second, test yourself instead of just reading your notes again.
Trying to remember information makes it stay in your memory longer.
Finally, get enough sleep, because your brain organises new information while you sleep.
Try these tips for one week and see the difference.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: We need to choose something for the team event next month. Any ideas?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: How about a cooking class? Everyone works together, and we eat at the end.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That's a good idea, but it might be expensive for twenty people.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: True. What about a picnic by the lake? It's free, apart from the food.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: The weather could be a problem in April, though.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Then let's book the cooking class and ask the company to pay half.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: OK, I'll write to the manager today.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: So, how's the new apartment?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I love it. It's much bigger than my old place, and it's close to the station.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: What about the rent?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: It's a bit higher, but I'm saving money because I don't need the bus anymore.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Do you get on with your neighbours?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I've only met one. She's lived there for ten years and she's very friendly.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: You should have a party to meet the others.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Maybe once I've unpacked all the boxes!
Welcome to the Science Museum.
This guide will take you through our three main galleries.
On the ground floor, you'll find the space gallery, where you can see a real rocket engine.
The first floor is about the human body and has many hands-on activities for children.
Please note that photography with a flash is not allowed in the galleries.
The café on the second floor closes an hour before the museum, at four o'clock.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Our company is letting us work from home three days a week now.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Lucky you! Do you think you will be more productive?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Honestly, I'm not sure. I save an hour of travelling, but I get distracted easily at home.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Maybe you need a separate space to work in, not the kitchen table.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That's a good point. I also worry about losing touch with my colleagues.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: You could use the office days for meetings and teamwork, and keep the home days for focused tasks.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That makes sense. I'll try organising my week like that.
Around a third of all food produced in the world is never eaten.
In wealthy countries, much of this waste happens at home rather than on farms or in factories.
People often buy more than they need, especially when supermarkets offer deals like 'buy one, get one free'.
Another cause is confusion over date labels.
'Best before' only refers to quality, so food is usually still safe to eat after that date.
Planning meals for the week and checking the fridge before shopping can make a real difference.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Hello, I'm calling about an order I placed two weeks ago. It still hasn't arrived.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I'm sorry about that. Could you give me your order number?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: It's four, seven, two, nine, one.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Thank you. I can see the parcel was sent to your old address.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: But I updated my address in my account last month!

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: You're right, and I apologise. I'll send a new parcel today by express delivery, free of charge.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Thank you. Will I get a tracking number?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, you'll receive it by email within an hour.
The city council has announced that its bike-sharing scheme will double in size next spring.
Since it started two years ago, the scheme has recorded more than a million journeys.
However, some residents complain that bikes are often left blocking pavements.
To deal with this, riders will soon have to end their journeys at official parking points, or pay a fine.
The council also plans to add electric bikes, which will cost slightly more to rent.
Supporters say the changes will encourage more people to leave their cars at home.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: So, we've interviewed both candidates. Who do you think we should hire?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Clara has more experience, but Daniel seemed more enthusiastic about the role.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Experience matters, though. The project starts in three weeks and there's no time for long training.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: True, but Clara asked for a salary well above our budget.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Could we offer her a smaller salary with a bonus at the end of the project?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: It's worth trying. If she says no, we'll offer the job to Daniel.
Scientists used to think that sleep was simply a time for the body to rest.
We now know that the brain is surprisingly active during the night.
During deep sleep, it removes waste products that build up while we are awake.
Lack of sleep has been linked to poor concentration, weaker memory and a higher risk of illness.
Adults generally need between seven and nine hours a night.
Yet surveys suggest that a third of adults regularly sleep less than that.
Urban planners have long treated parks as a pleasant extra, something to add once the essential infrastructure is in place.
That view is increasingly hard to defend.
A growing body of research links access to green space with lower stress levels, better mental health and even reduced crime.
Trees also lower street temperatures by several degrees during heatwaves, which could save lives as summers become hotter.
The challenge is that land in city centres is extremely valuable, so councils face constant pressure to sell it to developers.
Some cities have responded creatively, turning disused railway lines and rooftops into public gardens.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: We've reviewed your proposal, and while we like the design, the price is higher than we'd anticipated.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I understand. The figure reflects the custom software we'd be building specifically for your stores.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Would there be any flexibility if we committed to a three-year contract instead of one?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: There could be. A longer commitment would let us spread the development costs, so we might reduce the annual fee by around ten percent.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That's encouraging. We'd also need the system running before the holiday season.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That's ambitious, but feasible if we can sign by the end of this month.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Then let's aim for that. I'll take the revised figures to our board on Thursday.
More and more companies now use algorithms to screen job applications before a human ever reads them.
Supporters argue that software is faster and, in theory, less prone to personal prejudice than a tired recruiter.
Critics point out, however, that an algorithm trained on past hiring decisions may simply learn to repeat past biases.
In one widely reported case, a system downgraded applications that mentioned women's sports clubs.
The question, then, is not whether to use these tools, but how to audit them.
Several governments are now considering rules that would require companies to explain how automated decisions are made.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Your town has seen visitor numbers triple in five years. Is that good news?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Economically, yes. Hotels and restaurants are thriving, and young people no longer need to leave to find work.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: But I gather not everyone is pleased.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That's right. Rents have soared because so many flats are now let to tourists, and some families have been priced out entirely.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: What is the council doing about it?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: We've introduced a cap on short-term rentals in the old town, and a small tourist tax that funds affordable housing.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Has it made a difference?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: It's early days, but rents have at least stopped rising.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I've been going through the survey results, and something doesn't add up.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: In what way?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Customers say price is their main concern, yet our cheapest product is the one selling worst.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Perhaps people say one thing and do another. Price might be what they think they ought to care about.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Or the packaging makes it look low quality, so they assume it won't last.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That's plausible. We could test it by selling it in different packaging in a few stores for a month.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Good idea. If sales rise, we'll know packaging is the issue rather than the price.
Traditional economics assumed that people make rational choices based on all available information.
Behavioural economists have shown that, in practice, our decisions are heavily shaped by how options are presented.
For example, when employees are automatically enrolled in a pension plan, with the option to leave, participation rises dramatically.
Nothing about the plan itself has changed; only the default has.
Governments have embraced such 'nudges' because they are cheap and preserve freedom of choice.
Critics, though, warn that the same techniques can easily be used to manipulate rather than to help.
